rationale:
Today's slate is built around the biggest GLP-1 story this week: the retatrutide TRIUMPH-2 results, published in The Lancet and presented at EASD on 29 Sep (momentum 92). It's the only long-form piece, and it has enough depth for 8–15 minutes: what a triple agonist is, the exact population (adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes), and why people with diabetes usually lose less. S1 is a spin-off of L1. It covers why people can't get retatrutide yet and why the "research peptide" versions sold online are risky. That topic is marked caution, so it has a safety-first angle and never names sellers or doses. Search for "buy retatrutide" will spike this week, so it's useful protection for viewers, and it sends traffic to L1.

The other pieces are spread across pillars and body systems:
- **S2 (lungs):** semaglutide and fewer asthma attacks and COPD flare-ups, framed as an early observational signal compared against sulfonylurea users.
- **S3 (practical habit):** throwing away GLP-1 pens safely. It's emerging, has almost no competition, and uses the NYC figures while keeping "officials suspect" wording.
- **C1 (gut):** evergreen tips for nausea and constipation, refreshed with the October 2026 expert review.
- **C2 (myth-bust):** tirzepatide vs semaglutide 7.2 mg. It corrects the "head-to-head" headlines by explaining indirect comparisons, and it never gives switching advice.

Mix: about 4 of the 6 pieces are emerging, rising or peaking; C1 is an evergreen topic with a timely hook; C2 is the myth-bust. Pillars used: research, is-it-for-you, beyond-weight, life-on-glp1, get-the-most and results, with none repeated. No organ or body system appears more than once apart from general metabolism.

I skipped these because we covered them in the last 30 days: hair loss, pancreatic cancer, stopping GLP-1s, CagriSema, the pill comparison, non-responders, muscle and sleep apnea. I deprioritized COMPETE SWITCH (the switching and dose framing is too close to our guardrails) and creatine (the direct evidence is thin).

Following the analytics playbook, every title states the real number with its population and comparator. All three Shorts are marked for 35–50s cuts so we can compare lengths.

pieces.topic: Retatrutide TRIUMPH-2 phase 3 (The Lancet, EASD 2026): 1,152 adults with obesity AND type 2 diabetes lost 12.7%, 19.1% and 20.8% on average at 80 weeks across the three dose arms vs 4.0% on placebo; A1C down by up to 1.6 points from a 7.7% baseline
pieces.angle: Keep the angle, with these changes. (a) Describe the population exactly as the paper's inclusion criteria do: adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity (or overweight, if the paper includes it). Use the analysed n from the paper. (b) Show 12.7% / 19.1% / 20.8% (raw mean, lowest, middle and highest dose arms) vs 4.0% on placebo at 80 weeks. Label them raw, and give placebo-adjusted differences only if the paper reports them. (c) Give A1C as up to −1.6 points from 7.7% (about 61 mmol/mol) vs −0.2 on placebo. (d) State that the trial is Lilly-sponsored and that retatrutide is investigational and not approved anywhere as of September 2026. (e) Take GI side-effect and discontinuation rates only from the Lancet paper, with the placebo rate next to each. Title: 'Retatrutide: 20.8% Average Weight Loss at 80 Weeks vs 4.0% on Placebo in Adults With Type 2 Diabetes and Obesity (TRIUMPH-2)'.
pieces.working_title: Retatrutide: 20.8% Average Weight Loss at 80 Weeks vs 4.0% on Placebo in Adults With Type 2 Diabetes (TRIUMPH-2)
pieces.why: Highest-momentum topic (92) with a Lancet paper and mainstream coverage in the last 24h. Search is spiking, and a precise, population-exact explainer stands out from the 'up to 60 pounds' headlines. | fact-check: Core numbers verified. The TRIUMPH-2 paper is in The Lancet ('Retatrutide in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes (TRIUMPH-2)', PII S0140-6736(26)01861-1), and the results were presented at EASD 2026 in Milan. Lilly reports mean weight loss of 12.7%, 19.1% and 20.8% across the three dose arms vs 4.0% on placebo at 80 weeks. A1C fell by up to 1.6 points from a 7.7% baseline, vs 0.2 points on placebo. The Lancet page returned a 403, so I couldn't confirm n=1,152 or the GI adverse-event rates. The scriptwriter must take both from the paper or the Lilly release, or drop them. There is also a scope issue: Lilly describes the population as 'type 2 diabetes and obesity or overweight', while the Lancet title says 'obesity'. Use the paper's exact inclusion criteria. The angle's raw vs placebo labels, the 'lowest/middle/highest dose arm' naming, the investigational status and the no-buying rule are all good. Add that the trial is Lilly-sponsored. Add the placebo A1C change (0.2 points) next to the 1.6. A 7.7% baseline is about 61 mmol/mol. SURMOUNT-2 and STEP 2 must be clearly labelled as separate trials with different drugs, doses and durations (72 and 68 weeks), not a comparison. Hedge approval status 'as of September 2026'. Verified sources: https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(26)01861-1/abstract ; https://investor.lilly.com/news-releases/news-release-details/lillys-triple-agonist-retatrutide-delivered-substantial-weight ; https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/blockbuster-retatrutide-trial-signals-a-new-high-water-mark-for-weight-loss-drugs/

pieces.topic: Retatrutide isn't approved yet: why online 'research peptide' retatrutide isn't the trial drug and why regulators are concerned
pieces.angle: Protective, evidence-first, one sharp idea. 'The ~21% result came from a controlled trial drug. The vials sold online are not that.' As of September 2026 retatrutide is investigational, with no approval from FDA, EMA or MHRA. Products labelled 'research use only' aren't made or tested for people, and regulators have warned about unapproved GLP-1 products (cite the FDA page directly, not the aggregator). Never name sellers, show products, or mention doses or sourcing. The better route: ask your doctor about approved GLP-1 options or a clinical trial. Point to the full L1 video. Exact prescriber line. Cut to 35–50s.
pieces.working_title: Retatrutide Isn't FDA-Approved as of Sept 2026: What 'Research Peptide' Vials Really Are #shorts
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1. It drives traffic to the long video and gives people searching 'buy retatrutide' trustworthy safety content. The radar marked it caution, so it's strictly safety-first.

pieces.topic: Semaglutide linked to about 40% fewer asthma attacks and about 20% fewer COPD flare-ups vs sulfonylurea users (UK health records, ERS Congress 2026)
pieces.angle: 'An early lung signal, not a new use.' In UK health records, people with asthma or COPD who started semaglutide had up to 40% fewer asthma attacks and about 20% fewer COPD flare-ups than people who started a sulfonylurea. Both are relative figures, and no absolute numbers were reported. On-screen qualifier: 'vs sulfonylurea starters · observational · UK records · conference data (ERS 2026)'. Say that other GLP-1s didn't show the same link. Airway inflammation is a hypothesis only. The researchers say this shouldn't change treatment on its own, so keep your inhaler plan and don't start a GLP-1 for your lungs. Exact prescriber line. Title: 'Up to 40% Fewer Asthma Attacks With Semaglutide vs Sulfonylureas in UK Records (Observational) #shorts'.
pieces.working_title: ~40% Fewer Asthma Attacks in Semaglutide Users vs Sulfonylurea Users (Observational) #shorts
pieces.why: Low competition, barely on YouTube, and timely as autumn virus season brings asthma flare-ups. It covers the lungs, a body system we haven't used lately, and has a stated number for the title. | fact-check: The source exists: ERS press release, 8 Sep 2026, ERS Congress in Barcelona. It reports UK electronic health records, four parallel new-user studies of about 20,000–22,000 people each, and GLP-1 RA starters vs sulfonylurea starters among people with asthma or COPD. The figures are framed as 'up to 40%' fewer asthma attacks and a 20% reduction in COPD flare-ups. Several things in the proposal need fixing. (1) '~40%' should read 'up to 40%': secondary coverage (HCPLive, Pharmacy Times) gives roughly 30–38% for semaglutide across analyses. (2) The ERS release does not state that participants had type 2 diabetes. The sulfonylurea comparator implies it, but don't write 'adults with type 2 diabetes' unless the abstract says so. Use 'people with asthma or COPD starting semaglutide vs a sulfonylurea (both diabetes medicines)'. (3) The release gives no absolute event numbers, so say that relative figures are all that's available. (4) Coverage reports that other GLP-1s (e.g. liraglutide) showed no significant association. Keep this in, so the finding isn't generalised to all GLP-1s. (5) Use the investigator's own caveat: findings 'should not change treatment decisions on their own', and people shouldn't start a GLP-1 for their lungs outside prescribing guidance. Conference data, not peer-reviewed. The inflammation mechanism is a hypothesis only. Verified sources: https://www.ersnet.org/news-and-features/news/weight-loss-injection-semaglutide-can-reduce-asthma-attacks-by-up-to-40-per-cent/ ; https://www.healio.com/news/allergy-asthma/20260914/semaglutide-associated-with-lower-exacerbation-risks-in-asthma-copd ; https://www.hcplive.com/view/semaglutide-cuts-asthma-attacks-by-up-to-40-real-world-study

pieces.topic: Throwing away GLP-1 pens safely: NYC sanitation needle-stick injuries hit 57 so far in 2026 vs 51 in all of 2025, and officials suspect rising injectable GLP-1 use
pieces.angle: A kind, practical 30-second habit. Pen needles count as sharps. Use an FDA-cleared sharps container or a heavy-duty plastic bottle with a screw lid, label it, never put it in recycling, and check local disposal rules (cite FDA's sharps disposal guidance). Keep 'officials suspect' wording for the GLP-1 link, and give 2026 as a 'so far' year-to-date figure. Frame it as protecting the people who collect your trash, with no shaming. Exact prescriber line. Cut to 35–50s.

pieces.topic: Making GLP-1 nausea and constipation easier: evidence-based habits from a new expert review of GI side effects (Nutrition in Clinical Practice, Oct 2026)
pieces.angle: Same framework, but source-tag the tips to the verified 2026 DMSO review and the expert consensus statements, not the unverified NCP October 2026 review. Slide 3 uses one named trial with its population, timeframe and placebo rate. The habits are: smaller meals, eating slowly, stopping at comfortably full, fewer high-fat or greasy meals, fluids, and gradual fibre. That's six, to match the title. Keep the red-flag slide and a no-dose prescriber slide. Title: 'GLP-1 Nausea & Constipation: 6 Habits Expert Reviews Say Can Help'.
pieces.working_title: GLP-1 Nausea & Constipation: 6 Habits a 2026 Expert Review Says Can Help
pieces.why: A high-volume evergreen question refreshed with a citable October 2026 review. The petrelintide 'fewer side effects' news keeps GI tolerability topical, and a checklist format gets saved. | fact-check: I couldn't verify the cited source. I found no 'Nutrition in Clinical Practice, Oct 2026' expert review of GI side effects. The nearest NCP item (doi 10.1002/ncp.70172) appears to be a narrative review of GLP-1 RA effects on nutrient intake. Its date and scope couldn't be confirmed (the page returned a 403). Don't build the carousel on it unless the writer confirms the exact title, date and that it covers these tips. Verified alternatives that support the same habits: (1) the 2026 Dove Press DMSO review 'Gastrointestinal Adverse Effects of GLP-1 and Dual GLP-1/GIP Receptor Agonists'. It recommends smaller, more frequent meals, avoiding high-fat or spicy foods, stopping at early fullness, and adequate fluids and fibre. It notes GI effects are mostly mild to moderate, dose-dependent and transient. (2) The 2022 multidisciplinary expert consensus on managing GI adverse events (PMC9821052). (3) The expert Delphi consensus on nutritional and lifestyle supportive care (PMC12768930). For slide 3, use one named trial with its placebo rate, e.g. STEP 1, semaglutide 2.4 mg, adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes, 68 weeks: nausea 44% vs 17% on placebo, constipation 24% vs 11%. Verify these against the NEJM paper, and don't pool figures from different trials. Make the habit count in the title match the slides exactly. Keep slide 8 to 'your prescriber can adjust your plan', with no dose-reduction or re-titration wording, even though the reviews mention it. Verified sources: https://www.dovepress.com/gastrointestinal-adverse-effects-of-glp-1-and-dual-glp-1gip-receptor-a-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-DMSO ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9821052/ ; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12768930/

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide vs semaglutide 7.2 mg ('Wegovy HD'): 4.5 percentage points more average weight loss for tirzepatide's highest dose in a Lilly-sponsored indirect comparison of SURMOUNT-1 and STEP UP (adults with obesity, EASD 2026)
pieces.angle: 'Tirzepatide vs semaglutide 7.2 mg: what an indirect comparison can and can't tell you.' Slides: (1) the question; (2) what an ITC is: two separate trials, statistically adjusted, not randomized against each other; (3) 4.5 points (highest dose) and 3.2 points (middle dose) more average weight loss for tirzepatide, with the qualifier 'indirect · Lilly-funded · adults with obesity without T2D · 72 weeks · treatment-regimen estimand · conference data'. Add on the same slide: 'On-treatment analysis: difference not statistically significant.' (4) each trial's raw average, labelled as separate trials; (5) the one true head-to-head, SURMOUNT-5, vs semaglutide 2.4 mg, with its population and timeframe, instead of the unverified Int J Obes item; (6) what matters for you: health conditions, tolerability, coverage and access; (7) questions for your prescriber. No verdict and no switching advice. Title: 'Tirzepatide vs Semaglutide 7.2 mg: 4.5 Points More Weight Loss in a Lilly-Funded Indirect Comparison, Not Head-to-Head'.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide vs Semaglutide 7.2 mg: 4.5 Points More Weight Loss, but It Wasn't Head-to-Head
pieces.why: 'Zepbound vs Wegovy' is a perennial high-volume search with a fresh EASD hook. Consumer explainers haven't caught up, and the honest 'not head-to-head' correction is our contrarian-but-true piece. | fact-check: The core figures check out: Lilly release (PR Newswire, 29 Sep 2026) and EASD 2026 abstract. The indirect treatment comparison used SURMOUNT-1 data (a subgroup, per the abstract) and STEP UP, in adults with obesity (BMI ≥30) without type 2 diabetes, at 72 weeks. Mean differences were −4.5 points for tirzepatide 15 mg and −3.2 points for 10 mg (treatment-regimen estimand). The analysis was Lilly-funded. Raw averages: 20.2% in SURMOUNT-1 (15 mg) and 13.7% in STEP UP (7.2 mg). Two things the angle leaves out would change how viewers read it. (1) Using the efficacy estimand (on-treatment), the difference was NOT statistically significant (1.8 points for 15 mg). That has to go on the result slide. (2) A real head-to-head trial exists, SURMOUNT-5 (tirzepatide vs semaglutide 2.4 mg, NEJM 2025). 'Which works best? This isn't head-to-head' must say there's no head-to-head against 7.2 mg, not that no head-to-head exists at all. I couldn't find the 'independent Int J Obes indirect comparison (28 Sep)'. Search only turned up Int J Obes ITCs in type 2 diabetes (SURMOUNT-2 vs STEP 2). Drop slide 5 unless the writer confirms the exact paper, date, population and that it compares against 7.2 mg. The 20.2% SURMOUNT-1 figure may be for the full trial rather than the subgroup used in the ITC, so label it as such. Avoid the 'Wegovy HD' brand as a lead. Verified sources: https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/lillys-zepbound-tirzepatide-10-mg-and-15-mg-was-associated-with-more-weight-loss-than-wegovy-hd-semaglutide-injection-7-2-mg-in-a-new-indirect-treatment-comparison-302892601.html ; https://endo2026.endocrine.org/ajaxcalls/PresentationInfo.asp?PresentationID=1845277
